title: When It Comes To College, Stop Looking for Fit
author: Horn, Michael B.
summary: Michael Horn argues that the popular college-advising mantra to 'find your fit' is well-intentioned but functionally useless for most teenagers, who research shows don't yet have a clear sense of their own values or why they're going to college at all. Because 17- and 18-year-olds are still forming their identities, many different college environments could genuinely fit them, which leaves them without real guidance and prone to defaulting to rankings or proximity. Horn's alternative, grounded in research for his book Choosing College, is to help students identify 'misfit' instead: environments they can clearly recognize as non-starters, since people are much better at recognizing what they don't want than articulating what they do. This reframes college search around ruling out clear mismatches in geography, size, academics, and campus culture rather than chasing an undefinable ideal.
points: Most high schoolers cannot define their ideal college fit because at 17-18 they are still discovering their own identity and values.
Research for 'Choosing College' found most students don't have a clear sense of why they're attending college in the first place.
People are consistently better at recognizing what they don't want than articulating what they do want — this is the basis for identifying 'misfit.'
Nearly 40% of students fail to complete a four-year degree within six years, partly because they can't identify environments where they're likely to struggle.
Practical alternative: have students dig into differentiating features (geography, size, academics, social scene) and flag personal non-starters rather than searching for a perfect match.
quotes: for most teenagers, that advice isn’t just unhelpful—it’s impossible to act on.
Most teenagers can’t define the perfect college for them. But they can usually recognize environments where they’d be unhappy.
most high schoolers don’t have a clear sense of why they’re going to college in the first place—or what they really value in a college.
just because many colleges could be a good fit doesn’t mean all will be.
When people lack experience, they’re often poor at describing exactly what they want. But they’re surprisingly good at recognizing what they don’t want.
